title: Packaging hierarchy — Image Wiki
text:
Packaging hierarchy
  Ordering what a pack says, under constraints no other graphic design job has — a reader who is standing up, holding it, deciding in seconds, from a metre away, next to fifty rivals, with part of the layout dictated by law.

  
    Termpackaging graphics hierarchy
    Also calledpack architecture, front-of-pack hierarchy, shelf impact, on-pack hierarchy
    Not the same aspackaging structure, brand identity, poster hierarchy
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Structure and graphics are two disciplinesThe far read and the near readVariant differentiation, and how it goes wrongThe law takes its cut firstThe clearest case study there isCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Stand in front of the breakfast cereal shelf. Forty or fifty packs, a metre away, and you will have picked one up before you have read a single word of it. What you actually used was a block of colour, a logo and one word.
Then you turn it over and the job changes. The pack is now 30 cm away, in your hand, and you want the fibre number, the allergens, whether this is the one with hazelnuts. Same six surfaces, two different reading problems.



Wolfmann, SPAR Tjøme, Norway, breakfast cereal shelves, 31 August 2023. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
Look at the AXA range in the second row and count what is identical: the red wordmark, the white oval it sits in, the position of that oval, the photograph of the contents filling the lower half, and a percentage in a circle. Only two things change between flavours — one word set in heavy capitals (BLÅBÆR, HASSELNØTT) and the colour of the band behind it (navy, plum, brown).
That is the hierarchy working: the constant part does the shelf-identification job at a metre, the two changing parts do the variant job, and the six-point strapline under the oval ("MED HAVRE OG SPRØ FLAKES") is only readable in the hand — which is where it belongs. Note also what is not on the pack: the price is on the shelf rail.


Structure and graphics are two disciplines
The first mistake is treating a pack as a picture. A pack is an object that is also a picture, and the two are designed by different people with different tools.
Packaging structure is the box, the tray, the closure, the tear strip, the cavity — how the thing opens and whether it survives a pallet. Packaging graphics is the printed surface. Microsoft's packaging team splits its own guidance into exactly these halves, "accessible structures" and "accessible graphics", and defines structural accessibility and graphic accessibility as separate terms (PACK-002, section 04). Their companion guide is blunt about letting them drift apart: a disconnection between three-dimensional and two-dimensional elements "runs the risk of creating unnecessary barriers to use and understanding".
You can see that failure on real packs: an arrow printed where there is no tab, a tear strip running through the ingredient panel, a resealable flap whose graphics give no hint it exists. Both halves are individually competent and the pack still fails, because the printed cue and the physical affordance point at different places.
The far read and the near read
The two jobs want opposite hierarchies, and they mostly get solved by geography: the front panel is tuned for the metre, the back and sides for the hand. A poster faces the same split, but a pack has an advantage a poster does not — you can turn it over.
This is not how packaging always worked. Until self-service shops, food was handed to you across a counter and the package barely had to speak. Sainsbury's opened its first self-service store in Croydon in 1950, and the Design Museum's account of what followed puts the mechanism plainly: in self-service stores, packaging design "took on a new importance as the only way of communicating information about the product" (PACK-011). Sainsbury's set up an in-house studio in 1963 under Peter Dixon; each designer was expected to deliver two or three package designs a week.



Clifford H. Poland, Interior view of a Piggly Wiggly self-service grocery store, 1918. Library of Congress, public domain. The credit line "©1918 Clarence Saunders" is printed on the original photograph.
The moment the problem was invented. Shelves are open, the counter clerk is gone, and for the first time a shopper is alone with the packages. Now look at what the packages are doing about it: nothing. Every can carries a small paper label with a wreath and a paragraph of roman type, all at the same weight, so from where the camera stands you cannot tell one from another — the shopkeeper's numbered signs hanging from the shelf edge ("SECTION 2") are doing the identification work instead.


Variant differentiation, and how it goes wrong
A range wants to look like a range. Push that too far and the shopper buys 400 mg when they wanted 200 mg, decaf when they wanted caffeinated, or the cat food instead of the dog food. The consistency that makes the brand findable at a metre is the same consistency that hides the difference at 30 cm.
The fix is boring and reliable: make the variant carry more than one signal at once. Colour and a word and position, so that a shopper who is colour blind, or in bad light, or holding a pack that faded in the window, still has something left to read. Microsoft states the same rule for functional information on a pack — colour must not be the only thing carrying the meaning (PACK-002). Treat "one colour per variant" as a starting point, not a law; it fails as soon as the range outgrows the supply of distinguishable colours.
The law takes its cut first
Some of the layout is not yours. Net quantity, ingredients, allergens, a nutrition table, a barcode — these arrive with sizes attached and do not shrink when the pack does.

runs offthe panelSachet, 60 x 95 mmneeds 81% of the panel area, and still overruns itspace left overfor everything elseCarton, 160 x 200 mmneeds 15% of the panel areasame scale, same blocks

Both panels are drawn at the same scale, and the outlined blocks are identical in size — that is the whole point. The required block needs 81% of the sachet's back panel and overruns it; on the carton the same block needs 15% and leaves the rest free.
This is why the rules themselves provide escape hatches. Alongside the Standard Vertical format, the FDA's published set of Nutrition Facts layouts includes a Tabular Display for Small Packages and a Linear Display for Small Packages (PACK-008) — the regulator has already conceded that its own preferred block does not fit everything.


Designers try to buy the space back. Danone's Aqua Life bottle in Indonesia dropped its label entirely and embossed the bottle, which forced the barcode onto the cap (PACK-004). Lush sells unwrapped shampoo bars, which leaves nowhere to print an ingredient list, so they built a phone app that recognises the product and shows what a label would have said. Same move both times: when the mandatory content will not fit, move it to another surface, including a digital one.
The clearest case study there is


2006 label: Calories set small, beside Calories from Fat
2016 label: Calories in large bold type, Added Sugars added


FDA's own illustrations of the label before and after the 2016 update. Both public domain (US federal work). Read the layout, not the numbers: the sugars figures differ between the two examples.
Left, everything competes. "Calories 230" is set at the same size as "Total Fat", with "Calories from Fat 40" sitting next to it at equal weight, and a second table of 2,000/2,500-calorie reference values fills the bottom third.
Right, one number wins. "Calories" is large and bold, "230" is larger still and pushed to the right margin; "servings per container" moves above "Serving size", which is now bold on its own line. "Calories from Fat" is gone. "Includes 10g Added Sugars" is indented under "Total Sugars". Vitamins A and C are out; vitamin D and potassium are in, each with an actual amount beside its percentage. The reference table is replaced by one sentence of footnote.
The percentages moved too, on the same food: 8 g of total fat was 12% of a daily value in 2006 and is 10% now, because the Daily Values themselves were updated (PACK-008). A layout can be re-ranked without a single ingredient changing.


Every one of those is a hierarchy decision with a published reason and a compliance deadline — 1 January 2020 for manufacturers with $10 million or more in annual food sales, a year later for smaller ones. It is the only layout in the world you can read the argument for.
Common mistakes

"The front panel is the design." It is one of two. The back is read for longer, by a more motivated reader, and it is where a pack loses trust if it is a mess.
"Bigger logo, more impact." At a metre the limit is usually contrast against the background, not size. A mark 20% bigger inside the same busy field is not easier to find.
"Structure is engineering, not design." The tab, the cavity and the tear strip are read before any type is. See Packaging you can actually open.
"Consistency across the range is always good." The same consistency that gets you found gets you confused. Break it deliberately on the one attribute a shopper must not get wrong.
"The mandatory block can be shrunk to fit." It cannot, and it is usually the first thing a printer or a regulator checks.


Reading a pack in five steps

Stand back two metres, or squint. What is still legible is the real first read, whatever the designer intended.
Find the variant. How many signals separate it from its neighbour — colour, word, number, position? One is fragile.
Turn it over. Is the mandatory block laid out for reading, or dumped in the space left over?
Look for a printed cue with no physical counterpart: an arrow or a "peel here" pointing at nothing.
Find the barcode. If artwork crowds it, someone finds out at the till (Packaging you can actually open).
